title: A river of wind 9 km up has pushed airliners past 1,300 km/h over the ground
body: The polar jet stream is a narrow band of westerly wind, typically a few hundred kilometres wide and often less than 5 km deep, flowing around **9 km up** at about 180 km/h. It forms where cold polar air meets warm tropical air: the bigger the temperature difference, the faster the wind, and Earth's spin turns the flow eastward. Pilots ride it on eastbound trips and dodge it on the way back, and in February 2024 unusually strong jet winds pushed some airliners past 1,300 km/h relative to the ground.

slides.alt: Animated globe seen from above North America, with winds drawn as flowing streaks. A red and orange band of fast wind crosses Canada, then bends into deeper and deeper waves that drift east over the continent.
slides.caption: A computer model of winds in June and July 1988, sped up so a day passes about every second. The jet stream is the red and orange band, swinging into ever bigger waves as it flows east.

slides.label: jet stream winds this fast have been measured
slides.text: Its winds often exceed 92 km/h and typically blow at around 180 km/h.

slides.heading: Pan Am's first jet stream ride, Tokyo to Honolulu, 1952
slides.note: Flying at about 7,600 m on 18 November 1952 cut the trip by over a third

slides.heading: Found first, in Esperanto
slides.text: In the 1920s the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi detected the jet stream from a site near Mount Fuji. He published in Esperanto, so his work went largely unnoticed outside Japan. During the Second World War, Japan's Fu-Go balloon bombs were designed to ride the same winds across the Pacific.

slides.question: What makes the jet stream fastest in some places?
slides.explanation: The winds are strongest where the temperature difference between neighbouring air masses is greatest, which is why the jet runs along the edge of the cold polar air.
